This vignette works through a deployed extraction system from its published
counts. The source is Table 1 of Moldovan et al. (medRxiv
2026.05.18.26353541, DOI 10.64898/2026.05.18.26353541). A language model
extracted five fields from oncology notes. Three fields are scalar (one
value per note) and two are lists (several items per note).

```{r}
library(structeval)
```

## Counts in

Each row gives the pooled counts of correct (COR), incorrect (INC), missed
(MIS) and spurious (SPU) items, and the true negatives (TN) where the paper
reports them.

```{r}
table1 <- data.frame(
  field = c(
    "First Primary Diagnosis", "First Primary Histology",
    "First Primary Overall Stage", "Treatment Drugs",
    "Biomarker Test Results"
  ),
  type = c("scalar", "scalar", "scalar", "list", "list"),
  cor = c(154, 124, 88, 352, 301),
  inc = c(3, 5, 0, 0, 0),
  mis = c(1, 1, 6, 40, 41),
  spu = c(2, 0, 8, 55, 16),
  tn = c(40, 70, 98, NA, NA)
)
table1
```

For a scalar field every note adds exactly one of the five outcomes. The
counts therefore fix the per-note table, and the scalar rows can be expanded
note by note without loss. The paper does not report per-note counts for
the list fields. Here they are expanded to one item per row. That keeps
every pooled sum, and it encodes the item independence that the naive
interval assumes.

```{r}
expand <- function(row) {
  outcome <- c("cor", "inc", "mis", "spu", "tn")
  times <- unlist(row[outcome])
  times[is.na(times)] <- 0
  lab <- rep(outcome, times)
  m <- vapply(outcome, function(o) as.integer(lab == o), integer(length(lab)))
  data.frame(
    note = as.character(seq_along(lab)), field = row$field, type = row$type,
    m
  )
}
counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(table1)), function(i) {
  expand(table1[i, ])
}))
scalar_fields <- table1$field[1:3]
list_fields <- table1$field[4:5]
```

## Table 1 reproduced

Precision, recall, F1 and specificity are ratios of pooled counts. The
values below match the published table to the printed 0.1 percent.

```{r}
est <- metrics(counts, metric = c("precision", "recall", "f1"),
  method = "naive_wilson")
spec <- metrics(counts, field = scalar_fields, metric = "specificity")
point <- rbind(est, spec)[, c("field", "metric", "estimate")]
point$percent <- round(100 * point$estimate, 1)
point[order(point$field), c("field", "metric", "percent")]
```

## Intervals for the scalar fields

Precision, recall and specificity of a scalar field are note-level
proportions. Each note is one trial, so the Wilson score interval applies.
The published intervals came from a note-level percentile bootstrap.

```{r}
published <- data.frame(
  field = rep(scalar_fields, each = 4),
  metric = rep(c("precision", "recall", "f1", "specificity"), 3),
  published = c(
    "94.1-99.4", "94.8-99.4", "94.7-99.1", "87.8-100",
    "92.4-99.2", "91.4-98.5", "92.0-98.8", "100-100",
    "85.7-96.8", "88.2-97.2", "88.4-96.2", "87.0-97.1"
  )
)
sc <- metrics(counts, field = scalar_fields,
  metric = c("precision", "recall", "f1", "specificity"), seed = 2026)
sc$interval <- sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", 100 * sc$lower, 100 * sc$upper)
merge(sc[, c("field", "metric", "method", "interval", "boundary")],
  published, by = c("field", "metric"), sort = FALSE)
```

Histology specificity shows the boundary case. The paper reported 100
(100-100), a zero-width interval from 70 of 70 notes. The Wilson interval
on the same notes is 94.8 to 100. The scalar F1 is a ratio with note-level
denominators of 0, 1 or 2, so the router gives it the cluster bootstrap with
BCa percentiles.

## Intervals for the list fields

List precision, recall and F1 pool items within notes. Items in one note
share the note's text and tend to be right or wrong together. The naive
Wilson interval treats every item as an independent trial. The published
note-level bootstrap resamples whole notes and keeps that correlation. The
naive interval is narrower.

```{r}
li <- metrics(counts, field = list_fields,
  metric = c("precision", "recall", "f1"), method = "naive_wilson")
li$published_lower <- c(80.7, 83.2, 83.4, 90.3, 82.4, 87.3) / 100
li$published_upper <- c(91.6, 95.4, 92.1, 98.4, 92.8, 94.7) / 100
li$naive <- sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", 100 * li$lower, 100 * li$upper)
li$published <- sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", 100 * li$published_lower,
  100 * li$published_upper)
li$width_ratio <- round(
  (li$upper - li$lower) / (li$published_upper - li$published_lower), 2
)
li[, c("field", "metric", "naive", "published", "width_ratio")]
```

The naive intervals are about half to two thirds as wide as the note-level
intervals (`width_ratio` is naive width over published width). A report that used
the naive interval would overstate the precision of these estimates.

## Certifying against 0.90

The threshold test asks whether a metric exceeds 0.90 with one-sided
alpha 0.025. The decision is that the lower bound of the 95% interval
exceeds 0.90. For the scalar fields the Wilson bound decides.

```{r}
tt <- test_threshold(counts, rep(scalar_fields, each = 3),
  metric = rep(c("precision", "recall", "specificity"), 3), theta0 = 0.90)
tt$lower <- round(tt$lower, 3)
tt$p_value <- signif(tt$p_value, 2)
tt[, c("field", "metric", "estimate", "lower", "p_value", "reject")]
```

For the list fields the published note-level lower bound decides.

```{r}
li$certifies_090 <- li$published_lower > 0.90
li[, c("field", "metric", "published", "certifies_090")]
```

Only biomarker precision certifies. The F1 of both list fields falls short.

## Omissions against commissions

Treatment Drugs has 40 missed and 55 spurious items. Biomarker Test Results
has 41 missed and 16 spurious. The binomial test compares the missed share
with one half and treats items as independent.

```{r}
asym <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list_fields, function(f) {
  test_asymmetry(counts, f, method = "binomial")
}))
asym$estimate <- round(asym$estimate, 3)
asym$p_value <- signif(asym$p_value, 2)
asym[, c("field", "estimate", "n", "p_value", "reject")]
```

The biomarker field misses more than it adds. The drug field shows no clear
imbalance.

The clustered tests need per-note counts, which the paper does not report.
They are shown here on simulated notes that resemble the biomarker field:
100 notes, about 4 reference items each, within-note correlation 0.2, and
about 0.4 spurious items per missed item.

```{r}
sim <- simulate_counts(n = 100, theta = 0.88, m = 4, rho = 0.2,
  spu_ratio = 0.4, type = "list", seed = 2026)
rbind(
  test_asymmetry(sim, "field", method = "signflip", seed = 1),
  test_asymmetry(sim, "field", method = "cluster_t"),
  test_asymmetry(sim, "field", method = "binomial")
)[, c("method", "estimate", "p_value", "reject")]
test_threshold(sim, "field", "f1", theta0 = 0.80, seed = 1)
```

The sign-flip test works on the per-note difference between missed and
spurious items. A substitution adds one of each to the same note, so it
leaves the test unchanged.

## Planning the next validation

Three planning questions follow. Each asks for 80% power at one-sided alpha
0.025.

1. How many notes are needed to certify a scalar recall of 0.90 when the
   true value is 0.95?
2. The same question for a field present in 79% of notes, the prevalence
   of the diagnosis field (158 of 200).
3. How many notes are needed to certify a list F1 of 0.85 when the true
   value is 0.90, with 4 items per note and within-note correlation 0.2?

```{r}
rbind(
  n_threshold(0.90, 0.95),
  n_threshold(0.90, 0.95, prevalence = 158 / 200),
  n_threshold(0.85, 0.90, m = 4, rho = 0.2)
)[, c("theta0", "theta1", "m", "rho", "prevalence", "deff", "n_units",
  "n_present", "n_notes")]
```

The list design counts items, inflates them by the design effect, and
divides by the items per note.

A small sample sets a hard limit on what it can certify. With 50 notes the
smallest count whose Wilson lower bound exceeds 0.90 is:

```{r}
min_certifiable(50, 0.90)
```

Only a perfect 50 of 50 certifies 0.90. A result of 49 of 50 gives a lower
bound of 0.895.
